lessonTitle: Using Clinical Guidelines: Locating Guidance, Weighing Evidence and Departing Appropriately

blocks.text: Two doctors in neighbouring clinics treat the same kind of patient with different drugs and both say they are following the guidelines. One is quoting an out-of-date local leaflet, the other the current national guideline. Knowing where guidance comes from, how strong its evidence is and when a patient legitimately falls outside it is part of safe prescribing.

blocks.markdown: A **clinical guideline** is a set of systematically developed recommendations that help clinicians and patients decide on appropriate care. National bodies publish most guidelines for prescribers: for example the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) in the United Kingdom, the British National Formulary (BNF) for drug information, and professional societies and bodies such as the US Preventive Services Task Force elsewhere. Hospitals and health boards add local guidance and formularies that adapt national advice.

items: Start with the national guideline body for the condition and read the current version and its date
Use the formulary or drug compendium (such as the BNF) for doses, cautions and interactions
Check whether local guidance or the local formulary changes the choice, for example because of antimicrobial resistance patterns
Check that the guideline covers the patient's age group, setting and comorbidities
Look at the strength of each recommendation and the quality of its evidence

blocks.title: Evidence hierarchy and certainty
blocks.text: For questions about treatment effects, evidence is ranked: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials, then individual randomised controlled trials, then cohort studies, case-control studies, case series and finally expert opinion. The GRADE approach rates certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low, and recommendations as strong or conditional (weak), by weighing benefit, harm, certainty, values and resources.

rows: Quality depends on the trials included
Confounding; treated and untreated may differ
blocks.caption: Types of evidence for treatment questions.

blocks.latex: RR=\frac{\text{event rate in treated}}{\text{event rate in controls}}\qquad \text{Events prevented per 1000}=1000\times p_c\times(1-RR)
blocks.caption: p_c is the baseline (control) event rate as a fraction; RR below 1 means fewer events with treatment.

blocks.title: Reading the size of an effect
blocks.prompt: In a trial 30 of 400 treated patients and 50 of 400 controls have a stroke. Calculate the relative risk, and the number of strokes prevented per 1000 patients if the baseline risk is 5% and the same relative risk applies.
blocks.answer: RR 0.60. At 5% baseline risk about 20 strokes are prevented per 1000 treated; the same RR prevents more events in higher-risk patients.

blocks.markdown: **Justifying a drug choice.** A defensible justification names the guideline or study, states the type and certainty of evidence, the size of effect on outcomes that matter to patients (mortality, events, symptoms rather than only surrogate markers such as blood test changes), the harms, and the applicability to this patient. A narrow 95% confidence interval that excludes no effect (RR 1) suggests a real effect, whereas a wide interval that includes 1 means the data are compatible with no benefit. Strong recommendations backed by high-certainty evidence carry more weight than conditional recommendations from low-certainty evidence.

**Departing from a guideline.** Guidelines describe what is appropriate for most patients, not every patient. Departure may be justified by contraindication or allergy, drug interactions, pregnancy or breastfeeding, renal or hepatic impairment, frailty or limited life expectancy, a different evidence base for a subgroup, or an informed patient's preference. The departure should be a reasoned decision, discussed with the patient and documented, with the reason recorded, not a matter of habit.

blocks.title: Estimating events avoided at a different baseline risk
blocks.prompt: A guideline-recommended drug has RR 0.75 for hospital admission. A patient group has a baseline admission risk of 12% per year. How many admissions would be prevented per 1000 treated for a year?
blocks.answer: About 30 admissions prevented per 1000 patients per year.

rows: Severe penicillin allergy where a penicillin is first line
Use a guideline-listed safer drug or seek specialist advice
Renally cleared drug at low eGFR
Patient declines a treatment after discussion
blocks.caption: Legitimate reasons to depart from guidance.

blocks.title: Guidelines inform, they do not replace judgement
blocks.text: Locate the current national guidance, judge the strength of its evidence, apply it to the individual patient, and record the reason whenever you deviate.

points: Find the current national guideline and formulary, check its date and applicability, and be aware of local adaptations.
Justify choices using the evidence hierarchy, GRADE certainty, effect sizes such as relative risk and confidence intervals, and patient-relevant outcomes.
Depart from a guideline only for reasoned patient-specific circumstances such as allergy, pregnancy, organ impairment, frailty or preference, and document why.

questions.stem: Where should a prescriber first look for guidance on the recommended management of a common condition such as hypertension?

options.text: The current guideline from the national guideline body, with the formulary for drug details
A pharmaceutical company advertisement
A colleague's memory of past practice
An outdated textbook edition

questions.correctOptionText: The current guideline from the national guideline body, with the formulary for drug details

distractorRationale.c: Memory may be out of date.
distractorRationale.d: Old texts may contain superseded advice.

questions.explanation: National guideline bodies publish regularly updated, evidence-based recommendations. The formulary adds dosing, cautions and interactions.

questions.stem: Which feature most increases confidence in a guideline?

options.text: Systematic review of evidence, graded recommendations and declared conflicts of interest
A long list of author names
Being published only as a leaflet
Being sponsored by a single drug company

questions.correctOptionText: Systematic review of evidence, graded recommendations and declared conflicts of interest

distractorRationale.b: Length of author list does not indicate quality.
distractorRationale.d: Sponsorship by a single company raises bias concerns.

questions.explanation: A transparent systematic methodology with graded recommendations and declared interests allows users to judge reliability.

questions.stem: Which type of evidence sits highest in the usual hierarchy for treatment effectiveness?

options.text: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials
Case series
Expert opinion
Single case report

questions.correctOptionText: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials
questions.explanation: Pooling randomised trials reduces random error and bias from any one study, giving the most reliable estimate of treatment effect.

questions.stem: Drug A has a strong recommendation based on high-certainty evidence from several randomised trials showing fewer deaths. Drug B has a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty observational data and a laboratory marker. Which choice is best justified for a typical patient?

options.text: Drug A, because the evidence is stronger and concerns patient-important outcomes
Drug B, because it is newer
Either, because the evidence is equal
Neither, because guidelines are unreliable

questions.correctOptionText: Drug A, because the evidence is stronger and concerns patient-important outcomes

distractorRationale.b: Newness does not equal better evidence.

questions.explanation: High-certainty trial evidence on mortality is a stronger basis for a choice than low-certainty observational data and surrogate markers.

questions.stem: A guideline recommends a penicillin first-line for an infection, but the patient has a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Choose a guideline-listed alternative and document the reason for departing from first-line
Give the penicillin anyway because it is guideline first-line
Withhold all treatment
Ask the patient to choose without information

questions.correctOptionText: Choose a guideline-listed alternative and document the reason for departing from first-line

distractorRationale.d: Informed discussion is needed, not uninformed choice.

questions.explanation: Allergy is a legitimate reason to depart from the default recommendation. Most guidelines provide alternatives and the reasoning should be recorded.

questions.stem: Clinical guidelines are rigid rules that must be followed identically for every patient regardless of circumstances.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Guidelines describe appropriate care for most patients and require clinical judgement. Departures are acceptable with good reason, discussion and documentation.

questions.stem: In a trial 72 of 900 treated patients and 90 of 900 control patients have a hospital admission. Calculate the relative risk.
questions.explanation: The treated risk is 72/900 = 0.08 and the control risk is 90/900 = 0.10. The relative risk is 0.08/0.10, which is 0.80.

questions.stem: A treatment has relative risk 0.75 for stroke. In a group with baseline risk 12% per year, how many strokes are prevented per 1000 patients treated for a year?
questions.explanation: Without treatment 120 strokes are expected per 1000. The relative risk of 0.75 leaves 90, so 30 are prevented.

questions.stem: A new drug is supported by one small open-label trial that showed improvement in a blood marker. An older drug has several large randomised trials and a meta-analysis showing a reduction in cardiovascular events (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.91). Justify which you would prefer and explain what the numbers mean.
markingGuide: Older drug has higher-certainty evidence from multiple randomised trials and a meta-analysis
New drug trial small, open-label (risk of bias) and uses a surrogate marker
RR 0.82 means an 18% relative reduction in events
The CI excludes 1, so the effect is unlikely to be due to chance
Patient-important outcomes matter more than surrogate markers
Consider harms, cost and patient preference
questions.explanation: Good justification combines type of evidence, certainty, outcome relevance and effect size. Marking should reward interpretation of the confidence interval.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant has newly diagnosed hypertension. The general adult guideline recommends an ACE inhibitor first-line. Explain how you would locate relevant guidance and whether and why you would depart from the general recommendation.
markingGuide: Locate the national guideline for hypertension in pregnancy rather than the general adult guideline
Check the formulary or drug compendium for pregnancy cautions
ACE inhibitors are harmful to the fetus and are avoided
Choose an alternative listed in the pregnancy-specific guidance
Discuss risks and benefits with the patient
Document the reason for departing from the general recommendation
questions.explanation: The population differs from that covered by the general recommendation, so a specific guideline applies. Marking should reward appropriate sources, rationale and documentation.
